```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
HAS_SL <- requireNamespace("SuperLearner", quietly = TRUE)
HAS_MLR3 <- requireNamespace("mlr3", quietly = TRUE)
HAS_PARSNIP <- requireNamespace("parsnip", quietly = TRUE)
RUN_SL <- HAS_SL
RUN_MLR3 <- HAS_MLR3
RUN_PARSNIP <- HAS_PARSNIP
```

```{r status, echo = FALSE}
if (!any(c(RUN_SL, RUN_MLR3, RUN_PARSNIP))) {
  cat("Live framework demos skipped: SuperLearner / mlr3 / parsnip not ",
      "installed.\n")
}
```

`cudaGlmnet` ships thin adapters that expose its GPU Gaussian lasso solver
through three modelling frameworks. Every framework is an optional
`Suggests` dependency: nothing is a hard `Imports`, and each registration is
attempted from `.onLoad` behind a `requireNamespace` guard plus `tryCatch`,
so a missing framework (or a version whose extension API has drifted) never
stops the package from loading. The live chunks below run only when the
corresponding framework is installed.

## Shared limitations

- `cuda_glmnet()` supports only the **Gaussian** family. Adapters reject a
  non-Gaussian `family` with a clear error; binomial and sparse `x` are
  future work, not silently pretended.
- The `obsWeights` and `id` arguments passed by SuperLearner are currently
  **ignored, not yet supported**.
- The solver returns a whole lambda path, so a single-number prediction must
  pick one penalty. The adapters predict at the smallest fitted lambda (the
  least-regularised end of the path) by default; `s` can override this in
  `SL.cudaGlmnet()`. There are no tunable parsnip model arguments yet.

## SuperLearner

`SL.cudaGlmnet()` follows the `SL.*` naming convention. It fits with
`cuda_glmnet()` and returns `list(pred = <numeric>, fit = <object>)`; the
companion `predict.SL.cudaGlmnet()` method predicts from the stored `fit`.
SuperLearner discovers the function by name at run time. The wrapper is an
ordinary R function, so it can also be called directly without SuperLearner
installed — this is the path exercised by the package unit tests.

```{r sl-direct, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 5), 60, 5)
Y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.5)
out <- SL.cudaGlmnet(Y, X, X, family = gaussian(), nlambda = 10)
length(out$pred)
```

With SuperLearner present, the same function is used as a library learner:

```{r sl-usage, eval = RUN_SL}
library(SuperLearner)
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 5), 200, 5)
Y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
sl <- SuperLearner(Y = Y, X = as.data.frame(X),
                   SL.library = "SL.cudaGlmnet", family = gaussian())
predict(sl, newdata = as.data.frame(X[1:5, ]))$pred
```

## mlr3

When `mlr3` is installed, `.onLoad` registers an R6 class inheriting
`mlr3::LearnerRegr` under the key `regr.cuda_glmnet`, whose `.train` calls
`cuda_glmnet()` and whose `.predict` calls `predict()`. mlr3 dispatches these
as **private** R6 methods (`get_private(learner)$.train(task)`), so they are
defined in the class `private` list rather than `public`. No change to mlr3 is
needed; registration happens inside the downstream package.

```{r mlr3-usage, eval = RUN_MLR3}
library(mlr3)
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 5), 200, 5)
Y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
task <- as_task_regr(data.frame(y = Y, X), target = "y")
learner <- lrn("regr.cuda_glmnet")
learner$train(task)
learner$predict(task)
```

## parsnip / tidymodels

When `parsnip` is installed, `.onLoad` registers a `cuda_glmnet` engine via
`set_new_model()` / `set_model_mode()` / `set_model_engine()` /
`set_dependency()` / `set_encoding()` / `set_fit()` / `set_pred()`, using the
parsnip >= 1.x `value=` / `options=` API. The model type is named `cuda_enet`
on purpose: creating a model-spec function called `cuda_glmnet()` could
otherwise shadow this package's own solver. `cuda_enet()` is the shipped
constructor for that model specification.

The engine declares a **matrix** interface, so `fit_xy()` is the natural
entry point (the predictor matrix must have column names, a parsnip
requirement). The formula `fit()` path also works.

```{r parsnip-usage, eval = RUN_PARSNIP}
library(parsnip)
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 5), 200, 5,
            dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("V", 1:5)))
Y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
spec <- cuda_enet(mode = "regression", engine = "cuda_glmnet")
fit <- fit_xy(spec, x = X, y = Y)
head(predict(fit, new_data = X[1:5, , drop = FALSE]))
```

## Verification status

All three frameworks (`SuperLearner`, `mlr3`, `parsnip`) are installed on the
machine that produced this vignette, so the chunks above run live:

- The SuperLearner-style `SL.cudaGlmnet()` fit-to-predict path is verified by
  `tests/testthat/test-engines.R` (it needs no SuperLearner install) and by
  the live `sl-usage` chunk.
- The `mlr3` path is verified end-to-end: register -> train -> predict ->
  3-fold CV. The `.train` / `.predict` private-method requirement was found
  and fixed against real mlr3; a public-method definition registers but then
  fails at `train()` with "attempt to apply non-function".
- The `parsnip` path is verified end-to-end (register -> `fit_xy` / `fit` ->
  `predict`) against parsnip 1.6.1. That version replaced the 0.x
  `func=` / `defaults=` / `args=` registration with `value=` / `options=`;
  the engine was ported accordingly. On a 200 x 5 planted-signal problem the
  fitted predictions correlate with the response at ~0.97.

The roadmap (section 9) acceptance criterion has **two** halves: (1) at least
one framework runs register -> CV -> predict, and (2) it is faster than that
framework's `glmnet` engine. Half (1) is now met for mlr3. Half (2) is
**not** met: on single-fit tasks the GPU drop-in learner is much slower than
the `glmnet` engine, because it pays a fixed device setup cost that is only
recovered over a whole lambda path / many repeated fits. The measured
single-fit wall times (CUDA device, `n x p` Gaussian designs, median of 3)
were:

| scale | cuda_glmnet (s) | glmnet (s) | glmnet / cuda |
|-------|-----------------|------------|---------------|
| n = 200, p = 40   | 2.750  | 0.023 | 0.01x |
| n = 500, p = 200  | 4.648  | 0.039 | 0.01x |
| n = 300, p = 2000 | 11.818 | 0.085 | 0.01x |

These are a snapshot, not a guarantee. `cudaGlmnet`'s demonstrated advantage
is on **repeated-fit** workloads (whole lambda paths, CV folds, bootstrap
resamples, resident subset refits), not on one-off single fits — see the
`ridge-benchmark`, `bio-flagship-benchmark` and `subset-residency` vignettes.
The framework adapters exist so those workloads can be reached from mlr3 /
tidymodels / SuperLearner; they are not a claim that a single `fit()` call
beats `glmnet`.
